paragraphs.heading: A triangle of numbers
paragraphs.text: Pascal's triangle is an endless triangular array of numbers called binomial coefficients, which matter in probability theory, combinatorics and algebra. Its rows are counted from the top, starting with row 0, and the entries in each row are counted from the left, starting at 0. Row 0 holds a single 1. Every entry below it is the sum of the two numbers just above it, one up and to the left and one up and to the right, with any blank spot treated as 0.

paragraphs.heading: Building it by adding
paragraphs.text: So row 1 starts with 1, because 0 plus 1 is 1. Further down, the 1 and the 3 sitting next to each other in row 3 add up to the 4 in row 4. Each row also adds up to twice the row before it: row 0 totals 1, row 1 totals 2, row 2 totals 4. That doubling happens because every number feeds two numbers in the next row, one on its left and one on its right.

paragraphs.heading: Rows, subsets and chance
paragraphs.text: Put another way, the numbers in row n add up to 2ⁿ. This matches a counting fact: a set with n members has 2ⁿ subsets, since each member can be put in or left out independently. Divide row n by 2ⁿ and you get the binomial distribution for p = 1/2, the symmetric case. By the central limit theorem, that distribution comes closer and closer to the normal distribution as n grows.

paragraphs.heading: Multiplying out brackets
paragraphs.text: The triangle supplies the coefficients that turn up when a binomial expansion is written out. The coefficients at the two ends are always 1. Each inner coefficient of (x + 1)ⁿ⁺¹ is the sum of two neighbouring coefficients from the power before it, (x + 1)ⁿ, which is exactly the add-the-two-above rule. So instead of doing the multiplication, you can look the right entry up in the triangle, which is built from additions alone.

paragraphs.heading: Older than Pascal
paragraphs.text: The pattern was known long before Blaise Pascal, the French mathematician whose name it carries in much of the West. In India, the 10th-century commentator Halāyudha explained a method of Piṅgala's for counting metres that is equivalent to the triangle. In Persia, al-Karajī (953–1029) described it in a book now lost, and Omar Khayyám kept that work alive and used the coefficients in a general method for finding nth roots, and in Iran it is called Khayyam's triangle. In China, Jia Xian knew it in the 11th century and Yang Hui defined it in the 13th, and there it is Yang Hui's triangle.

paragraphs.heading: How it got its Western name
paragraphs.text: Petrus Apianus printed the full triangle on the frontispiece of a book on business calculations in 1527. In Italy it is named after Tartaglia, who published six rows of it in 1556. Pascal's own treatise on the arithmetical triangle appeared in 1665, after his death; in it he brought together several results already known about it and used them to solve probability problems. The name came later, when Montmort in 1708 called it Pascal's table for combinations and Abraham de Moivre in 1730 called it Pascal's arithmetic triangle, the basis of today's Western name.
